Madison County's seat and biggest city, Rexburg, lies in eastern Idaho. Residents numbered 39,409 in the 2020 census, compared with 1,081 in 1900, and the median age was 22.8. Brigham Young University-Idaho explains that, and because houses near campus are often rented, some owners are landlords instead of residents.

Of 10,066 housing units in 2020, 12.1% were vacant. Homeowner vacancy was 0.9%, while rental vacancy was 13.0%, so rentals sit empty far more often than owner-occupied houses.

Madison School District 321 covers almost every Rexburg address. A few blocks fall in the Sugar-Salem Joint School District 322 instead. If you live near that edge, check the district first, then tell buyers.

In June 1976 the Teton Dam gave way. The Teton River passes through northern Rexburg, and the flood put most of the city under water for days. A museum on the subject, Teton Dam Flood, occupies the Rexburg Tabernacle basement.

Lenders and buyers want to know if a parcel sits in a mapped flood area. Your title company or insurer can give the flood status for your address. Any past water in the basement should be mentioned at the outset.

Winters are long and cold, summers short and dry. An average January day peaks at 29.5 degrees Fahrenheit and bottoms out at 14.2. Minus 36 is the record low, and every month of the year has seen frost.

Snow matters more than rain here. About 54.9 inches of snow falls in a year against 12.63 inches of total precipitation. The heaviest month on record brought 43.5 inches in December 1983, and the deepest snow cover, 38 inches, has happened twice, in March 1985 and February 2008. Three parts of a house take the stress:

  • Roofs: long snow cover and repeated freeze and thaw wear shingles, flashing and gutters.
  • Heating: a furnace that fails in January is an urgent repair, and buyers know it.
  • Plumbing: freezing is the usual risk for pipes in crawl spaces and outside walls.

Inspections catch aging roofs and furnaces, and the findings become repair requests. An as-is sale hands that risk to the buyer.

Two cases come up often. One is an investor whose student tenants have a lease ending in April or August and who wants to sell without disturbing them. The other is a family that inherits a long-rented house with maintenance put off.

Tenants do not have to leave for a sale to happen. The lease goes with the house and the buyer assumes its terms, so study it and any deposit duties before signing a contract.

City Ordinance 1308 and the Building department's short-term rental page set the rules: register with the city, pass a life safety inspection and renew yearly. Check them if your house has hosted nightly guests or your buyer wants to run it that way.

  • Zoning sets the occupancy rule. In the TAG, RR1, RR2, LDR1, LDR2 and LDR3 zones the owner or a manager must live on-site. In MDR1, MDR2, HDR1 and HDR2 the owner, a manager or the owner's agent must be available in Madison County.
  • Parking must cover two spaces for the house plus one more for each rented room.
  • Inspectors look at egress window sizes, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and a kitchen fire extinguisher, among other things.
  • Three violations of city ordinances at the property can lead to revocation of the registration.

Do not promise a buyer that a registration transfers until the city confirms it.

Payment comes in two halves, with the first due December 20 and the second due the following June 20. Reach the Treasurer's Office at 134 E Main, or at 208-359-6200, option 5.

DateWhat happens in Madison County
April 15Filing closes at the Assessor's Office for the Homeowners Exemption and Circuit Breaker
June 20Second half payable
Fourth Monday of JuneDeadline to protest your value with the Assessor
December 20First half, at minimum, payable

Late on the first half and you owe a 2 percent charge as of December 21, then interest at 1 percent monthly from January 1. The second half draws the 2 percent charge on June 21, yet its interest also runs from January 1 rather than June 21.

One bill covers the calendar year. If you close mid-year, the title company normally splits the current tax between you and the buyer. A bill that never arrived still leaves the tax owed.

Three unpaid years let the county take a deed to the property under Idaho Code 63-1002. It must first send certified mail to recorded interest holders and publish notice in a newspaper for four weeks. Under Idaho Code 63-1007, the owner may still redeem ahead of the sale by paying every delinquent year and the current one.

A sale that pays the county at closing stops that clock. Ask the Treasurer's Office for the balance in writing before accepting an offer.
Madison School District 321 serves nearly all of Rexburg, with six elementary schools: Adams, Burton, Hibbard, Kennedy, Lincoln and South Fork. Madison Memorial Hospital is just east of downtown.

Idaho closing steps are the same for cash, apart from the missing mortgage. Describe the house, get a written offer, then decide. A title company records the deed, clears liens and settles property tax.

Cash Home Buyers buys as-is and charges you no fees, commissions or closing costs. Turning down the offer costs nothing. Weigh the routes on three points:

  • Timeline: showings and loan approval drive a listing, while title work and your chosen date drive a cash sale.
  • Condition: roof, furnace and plumbing requests follow a listing inspection, not an as-is sale.
  • Costs: an agent's commission and seller closing costs usually come with a listing. Get both estimated in writing before you compare what you would net.

• Inherited house: settle who can sign, collect the death certificate and court papers, and look for unpaid taxes.
  • Behind on payments: request a payoff figure from the lender and the tax balance from the Treasurer.
  • Rental needing work: write up the repairs, read the lease, and decide whether tenants stay.

Bring the lease, your latest tax bill and a note about any past flood or water damage to your first conversation with a buyer. Those three items shape the offer more than anything else on a Rexburg house.

Nothing here is legal or tax advice. Check specifics with the county, an attorney or a tax adviser.

faqs.q: What is the property tax deadline in Rexburg?
faqs.a: Madison County splits the bill, with December 20 and June 20 as the dates. Lateness brings a 2 percent charge plus 1 percent interest each month.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Rexburg house that has student tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. The lease stays with the house and the buyer assumes it. Review it and any deposit duties before you sign.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to run a short-term rental in Rexburg?
faqs.a: Yes, registration is mandatory, along with a life safety inspection and yearly renewal. Certain zones want the owner or manager on-site, and three ordinance violations can cost you the registration.

faqs.q: What if I owe back taxes on a Rexburg house?
faqs.a: Start with the oldest delinquency, because the county applies payments in that order. Three years of nonpayment can end in a deed to the county, though redemption stays open until the sale if you pay every delinquent year and the current one.

faqs.q: Does Cash Home Buyers charge fees on a Rexburg sale?
faqs.a: No. Fees, commissions and closing costs are not charged to you, and declining an offer is free.
